messages.author: e7014f74b5d49111
messages.subject: Divergent transitions and low neff in Multinomial-Logistic Normal Model
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to infer a (relatively simple) Multinomial-Logistic Normal model. I am however having trouble as my sampler continues to have many divergent transitions (~545 from 4 chains each sampling 1000 samples) despite an adapt_delta=0.99. The plot for the variance does appear to be somewhat funnel shaped, but I am not sure what to do about this. I thought this type of model was fairly common based on reading some forum posts. 

I must admit, this is my first attempt at using stan and I am sorry if I am making a stupid mistake. 

Thank you very much for any advice you can provide!!!
Justin Silverman

b.  There's some Cholesky thing that can make the mulltivariate normal thing go faster.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Divergent transitions and low neff in Multinomial-Logistic Normal Model
parts:
I'd strongly suggest starting simpler in a new language.

You probably need a non-centered parameterization. There's an
explanation of how to do that in the manual in the section
titled "Hierarchical Models and the Non-Centered Parameterization".

We don't have efficient Wisharts because we don't use them.
The problem is that cov_matrix by itself can be very unstable.
It's much more numerically stable and efficient to use Cholesky
factors instead.

- Bob

messages.author: e7014f74b5d49111
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Divergent transitions and low neff in Multinomial-Logistic Normal Model
parts:
Thank you both very much for your help. In the end it was a combination of three things that solved the problem:

1) Using LKJ + Cauchy prior, rather than inverse wishart
2) Working with Cholesky Factorizations
3) Using a non-centered parameterization. 


This brings up a question though:

I actually have fairly strong prior information regarding one of the covariance terms in my model. For the KxK matrix sigma I have estimates for each of the terms sigma_ij.  When I was working with the Inverse Wishart it was clear to me how to encode this prior information into the inverse wishart parameters. However with the LKJ prior I really have no idea, this is the first I have heard of this prior and unfortunately web searches have offered up little. How could you encode this information into an LKJ prior? Is there some decomposition of sigma that would allow my LKJ + Cauchy prior match my prior information for the expected value of sigma? Should I just be using the inverse wishart in this situation?

Thank you again!
Justin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Divergent transitions and low neff in Multinomial-Logistic Normal Model
parts:
On Monday, March 6, 2017 at 9:12:08 AM UTC-5, Justin Silverman wrote:
This brings up a question though:

I actually have fairly strong prior information regarding one of the covariance terms in my model. For the KxK matrix sigma I have estimates for each of the terms sigma_ij.  When I was working with the Inverse Wishart it was clear to me how to encode this prior information into the inverse wishart parameters. However with the LKJ prior I really have no idea, this is the first I have heard of this prior and unfortunately web searches have offered up little. How could you encode this information into an LKJ prior? Is there some decomposition of sigma that would allow my LKJ + Cauchy prior match my prior information for the expected value of sigma? Should I just be using the inverse wishart in this situation?

The expectation of a LKJ-distributed correlation matrix is the identity matrix, and there is no way to change that within the LKJ framework. If you really want to provide the expectation, you could use the inverse Wishart and integrate the covariance matrix out

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-Wishart_distribution#Conjugate_distribution

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Divergent transitions and low neff in Multinomial-Logistic Normal Model
parts:
We're probably only going to do this very stably once
we have Wisharts parameterized for Cholesky factors:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/43

We should also include some discussion of how to exploit conjugacy with
multivariate models in the manual. I'll put that in longer
term manual issues:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1238#issuecomment-284615579

- Bob
